A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core algorithms, theorems, and illustrations. All pages are readable, including v2's new Appendices A–D; v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical bounds, proofs, and illustrative mathematical examples, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: Appendix C and Table 2 report an original synthetic experiment on time-varying uniform matroids, including regret, runtime, and confidence intervals.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain their steps. Appendix D adds an adaptation for uncorrupted feedback with tied objective components: contract strongly connected components and choose estimates constant within each component. The expanded centroid implementation details elaborate the approximation already contemplated in v1.

E1.justification: v2 introduces the first empirical task coverage: synthetic online inverse optimization over time-varying uniform matroids, with changing item availability. v1 discusses uniform matroids theoretically but does not evaluate them experimentally.

E2.justification: Table 2 introduces actual empirical comparisons against ONS from Sakaue et al. (2025b) and OGD from Bärmann et al. (2020). Neither was experimentally evaluated in v1; its related-work table only compared theoretical bounds.

E3.justification: Appendix C establishes the first experimental protocol: d = 20 items, 10 unavailable each round, selection of 5 available items, and T = 5000. It measures regret and per-round runtime and tests centroid approximations with 100, 1000, and 10000 hit-and-run iterations. These are settings for a new experiment.

E4.justification: Table 2 adds a focused sensitivity analysis varying the hit-and-run iteration budget. It examines how approximation effort affects regret and computational cost. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analysis.

E5.justification: v2 introduces averages over five independent trials and 95% confidence intervals for regret in Table 2. This uncertainty-reporting practice is limited to the new synthetic experiment; v1 reports no empirical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds six empirical result rows. Mean regret is 1.640 for quadratic Algorithm 1 and 1.677, 1.491, and 1.201 for its centroid variant at increasing iteration budgets, versus 3.510 for ONS and 4.848 for OGD. Runtime results reveal increasing computational cost with approximation effort. v1 has no corresponding measurements.

T1.justification: Appendices A–B add approximation-error, expected-regret, and explicit oracle-complexity derivations. Section 6 changes the randomized lower bound from R_T to E[R_T] and explicitly verifies the embedding preserves objectives and regret. Section 2.1 and Appendix D replace v1's blanket perturbation argument for ties with separate reasoning for uncorrupted and corrupted feedback.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: O(d log d) regret, O((C + 1)d log d) regret without knowing C, and an Omega(d) lower bound. The new appendices support and qualify these contributions without adding a new headline claim.

C2.justification: v1 describes distinct objective components as merely a technical convenience. v2 explicitly acknowledges that corruption detection requires distinctness because legitimate ties can also create cycles. Appendix D explains the uncorrupted exception. The conclusion additionally distinguishes this setting from inverse bandit learning, and Appendix C interprets the approximation-budget trend.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's general polynomial-time implementation discussion, Appendices A–C specify membership checks, interior-point initialization, approximation tolerances and failure probabilities, oracle costs, matroid greedy optimization, and experimental iteration budgets. v2 also supplies a code-repository link, substantially expanding implementation and reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v2 adds Sakaue (2026) to the logarithmic-regret discussion, Guha et al. (2024) and Petriconi and Vernade (2024) for inverse bandit connections, and Shioura and Tanaka (2007) for oracle algorithms. These are focused additions; the central positioning around M-convexity and finite regret remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose remain intact. v2 expands the lower-bound exposition, adds appendix cross-references and four appendix sections, and makes limited language, affiliation, equal-contribution, and acknowledgement edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 2, adjusts the sizing and spacing of Figures 1–2 while retaining their examples, and moves Algorithm 2 from page 12 to page 11. Table 1 accommodates an additional citation, and surrounding text reflows; the overall presentation format is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects v1's overbroad treatment of ties and clarifies that the randomized lower bound is in expectation. Its explicit approximate-centroid regret argument, computational analysis, and expanded lower-bound reduction materially improve the theoretical contribution's reliability and checkability. The new experiment and code link provide additional, narrowly scoped empirical and reproducibility support.
